subject: Career
title: Name Bias and Blind Resumes
description: A quick, practical guide to Name Bias and Blind Resumes.

hook.text: Identical resumes with different names get wildly different callback rates.

buildup.text: A famous study sent 5,000 resumes. 'White-sounding' names got 50% more callbacks.

discovery.text: This isn't conscious malice. It's implicit bias — fast judgments based on familiarity.

twist.text: Some companies now use blind resume screening, removing names and photos entirely.

climax.text: Orchestras did this first. Blind auditions behind screens doubled women's success.

quiz.question: What did blind auditions in orchestras achieve?

details.summary: Name bias is the documented tendency for resumes with traditionally white or male-sounding names to receive more callbacks than identical resumes with minority-associated names. Blind resume processes, which remove identifying information, help combat this systemic bias.
details.whyItMatters: Awareness of name bias empowers both candidates and employers. Candidates can advocate for fair processes, and employers can implement blind screening to reduce unconscious discrimination.
takeaways: Studies show identical resumes receive different callback rates based on name alone
Blind resume screening removes names and demographic indicators
Structured evaluation criteria reduce the impact of unconscious bias

faq.question: What does research say about the actual impact of name bias in hiring?
faq.answer: Landmark studies show that resumes with white-sounding names receive fifty percent more callbacks than identical resumes with Black-sounding names. Similar studies have documented bias against women's names for technical roles and against foreign-sounding names in many Western markets.

faq.question: What can job seekers do to mitigate potential name bias against them?
faq.answer: Focus on companies with demonstrated commitment to diversity, seek referrals that bypass initial screening, and apply through channels that use blind resume processes. Some candidates use initials or Anglicized names, though this is a personal decision with complex identity implications.
